steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
At a high level, a Transformer is a sequence‐to‐sequence model built almost entirely from two ingredients:  
  1. Self-attention modules (including multi-head attention)  
  2. Position-wise feed-forward networks  
and wrapped with residual connections and layer-normalization.  

Here’s a step-by-step, conceptual walk-through of the core ideas:

1. Tokenize & Embed  
   • Input text is split into tokens (words, subwords, characters).  
   • Each token is mapped to a learned vector (an embedding).  
   • Since the model has no built-in sense of word order, we add a “positional encoding” to each embedding so the model can tell first from last, near from far.  

2. Self-Attention: Let Tokens Talk to Each Other  
   • Self-attention lets each position in the sequence look at (attend to) every other position.  
   • For each token we compute three vectors (via learned linear projections):  
     – Query (Q)  
     – Key   (K)  
     – Value (V)  
   • Attention scores = (Q · Kᵀ) / sqrt(d)  (a measure of compatibility).  
   • Softmax over scores yields attention weights.  
   • Each token’s new representation = sum over all Value vectors weighted by those attention weights.  
   Intuition: “When processing the i-th word, look back at all other words, decide how much to borrow from each, then mix those borrowings into the new i-th representation.”  

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Instead of one Q/K/V projection, we do several in parallel (heads).  
   • Each head can focus on different relationships (e.g. syntax, long-range dependencies, local context).  
   • Their outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the original dimension.  

4. Position-Wise Feed-Forward  
   • After attention, each position is passed independently through a small two-layer feed-forward network (same weights for every position).  
   • This lets the model apply non-linear transformations and mix channels.  

5. Residuals & Layer-Norm  
   • Each sub-layer (attention or feed-forward) is wrapped as:  
       x → x + SubLayer(x) → LayerNorm(…)  
   • This stabilizes training, eases gradient flow, and helps the model go deeper.  

6. Stacking Layers  
   • You stack N identical “blocks” of (Multi-Head Attention → Feed-Forward) to form the encoder, and another stack for the decoder.  
   • Typical N is 6 or 12 in many language models, but you can go deeper.  

7. Encoder vs. Decoder  
   – Encoder: each layer does full self-attention over the entire input sequence.  
   – Decoder:  
     a. Masked self-attention over generated tokens so you can’t peek at the future.  
     b. Cross-attention that lets the decoder attend to encoder outputs.  
     c. Feed-forward, plus residuals & norm as usual.  

8. Final Prediction  
   • In language generation, the decoder’s top‐layer outputs go through a linear layer + softmax to predict the next token.  
   • During training you compare that prediction against the true next token and backpropagate.  

Why this works so well  
  • Parallelism: Unlike RNNs, all positions are processed simultaneously—no strict “one step at a time.”  
  • Flexible context: Each token can attend both locally and globally, at every layer.  
  • Scalability: Attention is a simple, highly optimized matrix operation.  

In brief, a Transformer learns how to mix information from every position in the sequence at every layer, then refines that information with small feed-forward nets—all the while preserving stability with residual connections and normalization. That combination of global context modeling + deep stacking is what powers state-of-the-art performance on translation, summarization, language modeling, and more.
